results.text:
Can a Power Station Run a Gas Furnace? How Long It Lasts 
 Skip to content 
 Can a portable power station run a gas furnace?
 Updated October 10, 2026 by Biel Vazquez 
 Short answer: Yes, if its inverter can start the blower: a ½ hp furnace blower runs on about 800 W but pulls about 2,350 W for a second as it starts. A 2,048 Wh station then keeps it going for about 4.4 hours when the blower runs half the time, 7.3 hours in mild weather and 3.1 hours in hard cold. Getting through an 8-hour night at 50% takes about 3.8 kWh of battery, so a power station bridges a short outage; a long one needs solar recharging or a generator.
 Runtime by power station size
 A gas furnace burns gas for heat, but it needs electricity for the control board, the igniter, the inducer fan and, above all, the blower that moves warm air through the ducts. Our calculators use 800 W running and 2,350 W starting for a ½ hp blower. How long a battery lasts depends on how much of each hour the blower actually runs, the duty cycle , which climbs as it gets colder outside:
 1,024 Wh station 2.2 h 
 2,048 Wh station 4.4 h 
 3,600 Wh station 7.7 h 
 5,000 Wh station 10.6 h 
 One night (8 h) 
 Hours of furnace blower (800 W) running half the time, 85% through the inverter, from a full battery. 
 Calculated with our runtime calculator, 85% efficiency through the AC inverter, battery run to empty. Power station 30% duty 50% duty 70% duty Running nonstop 
 1,024 Wh 3.6 h 2.2 h 1.6 h 1.1 h 
 2,048 Wh 7.3 h 4.4 h 3.1 h 2.2 h 
 3,600 Wh 12.8 h 7.7 h 5.5 h 3.8 h 
 5,000 Wh 17.7 h 10.6 h 7.6 h 5.3 h 
 Small stations around 1 kWh are a stopgap: about 2.2 hours at 50% duty, enough to keep a house from cooling off during a short outage, not to get through a night. It takes something in the 3.6–5 kWh range, usually a station with an expansion battery, to cover a night.
 Will it start the blower?
 Runtime is only half the question. A power station has two power limits on its spec sheet: a continuous rating and a surge (peak) rating that it can hold for a moment. The continuous rating has to cover the 800 W the blower draws while running, plus anything else on at the same time, and the surge rating has to cover the roughly 2,350 W it pulls as it starts. If the surge is too much, the station shuts its output off, however full the battery is.
 Your furnace's own blower may be smaller or larger. Look at the motor label inside the blower compartment: running watts are roughly the full-load amps (FLA) × 120 V. Many newer furnaces use a variable-speed ECM blower that ramps up gently and draws less while running, which makes both the start and the runtime easier on a battery. The generator guide for furnaces covers reading the label and the motor types in more detail.
 Furnace plus the fridge and internet
 In practice, the furnace shares the station with a refrigerator (200 W running, about 40% of the time) and the internet router (25 W). Their average draw adds up like this:
 Hours from a full station. Average draw = blower × duty + fridge × 40% + router. Furnace blower Average draw 1,024 Wh 2,048 Wh 3,600 Wh 5,000 Wh 
 Blower 30% of the time 345 W 2.5 h 5.0 h 8.9 h 12.3 h 
 Blower 50% of the time 505 W 1.7 h 3.4 h 6.1 h 8.4 h 
 Blower 70% of the time 665 W 1.3 h 2.6 h 4.6 h 6.4 h 
 The fridge costs less than you might expect, because a closed fridge in a cooling house rests most of the time. The blower is the load to manage.
 How much battery a cold night takes
 Working backward with our home battery calculator, this is the capacity needed for the blower alone, at 85% inverter efficiency:
 Blower duty Average draw For 8 hours For 24 hours 
 30% 240 W 2.3 kWh 6.8 kWh 
 50% 400 W 3.8 kWh 11.3 kWh 
 70% 560 W 5.3 kWh 15.8 kWh 
 A full day of heat at 50% duty needs about 11.3 kWh, about the size of a whole-home battery like the one in how long a 13.5 kWh battery lasts . To stretch a portable station: turn the thermostat down a few degrees, close doors to unused rooms, and recharge it in the day from solar panels or a generator. Winter sun is weak and short, so expect far less from a panel in December than in summer.
 Connecting a hardwired furnace
 A furnace is hardwired to its own 120 V circuit, so it has no plug to put into the station. The usual option is a single-circuit furnace transfer switch with an inlet, installed between the furnace circuit and the furnace, which you then feed with a cord from the station's AC outlet. Some larger stations are sold with their own transfer panels or are meant to feed a manual transfer switch; see interlock kit vs transfer switch . If the furnace lights, then shuts down after a few seconds, it may not be sensing its flame: the same neutral-to-ground issue that affects some portable generators can happen with some stations, so check the station's manual on how its output neutral is bonded.
 Calculate it for your station and furnace 
 Safety. Never plug a power station or generator into a wall outlet to feed the house: it can backfeed the utility lines and electrocute line workers. Use a transfer switch installed by a licensed electrician. And keep your furnace's outdoor intake and vent pipes clear of snow during a storm, with working CO alarms on every level of the home.

A furnace is wired straight into the house, so it needs a listed transfer switch, never a cord pushed into a wall outlet.

 Will a gas furnace work in a power outage?
 No, not a modern one. Carrier says a gas furnace needs electricity to power the blower fan, the electronic ignition and the internal control board. Bryant says the same about propane: in a power outage, a propane furnace will not run unless it is connected to a backup generator.
 Blower. Pushes the warm air through the ducts.
 Ignition. Lights the burners. No power, no flame.
 Control board. Carrier calls it the computer that runs the furnace and watches its safety sensors.
 If you heat with oil, the same connection rules on this page apply. The wattage figures below are for gas and propane furnace blowers, so read your oil furnace's own label.
 What a furnace draws
 Champion's generator wattage chart , the same chart our power calculator uses, lists a furnace fan (1/2 HP) at 300 to 800 W running and 800 to 1,600 W starting . The starting figure covers the moment the motor spins up.
 Real furnaces land inside that range. In a US Department of Energy Building America field study of eight furnaces near Syracuse, New York, the furnaces drew 371 to 750 W while heating with their original blower motors. After the researchers swapped in a brushless (variable-speed type) motor, the same furnaces drew 330 to 490 W .
 Furnace power, in watts 1,600 W Starting, top of Champion's range 
 800 W Running, top of Champion's range 
 750 W Highest heating draw in the DOE field study 
 Champion figures are for a 1/2 HP furnace fan. DOE figures are measured furnace draw in heating mode at eight homes.
 Read your furnace's label
 Find the amps on your furnace's rating plate or on the blower motor's nameplate, then multiply by 120 to get watts. The EZ Generator Switch FAQ uses this math: 120 volts x 3 amps = 360 watts running. Write your number on a card and keep it with your outage supplies. It tells you more than any chart.
 Find the furnace before the outage Know where the furnace, its service switch and its rating plate are while the lights still work. The amps on that plate decide which station or generator can run it.
 Add your furnace to the power calculator → Photo: user5974557 / Magnific Portable power station for a gas furnace: how long it lasts
 A power station can run a furnace if two things are true. Its rated output covers the furnace's running watts, and its surge covers the starting watts. All three stations below clear Champion's top figures (800 W running, 1,600 W starting) with room to spare. The question is hours.
 Start with stored energy. Use the maker's watt-hour (Wh) rating.
 Take 80% of it. This is the planning allowance for conversion losses that every calculator on this site uses.
 Work out the furnace's average draw. A furnace cycles on and off, and how much depends on the weather and the house. We have no single source for that share, so the table shows two examples: running nonstop, and running half the time.
 Divide. Usable watt-hours / average watts = hours.
 Example: the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 stores 2,042 Wh. 2,042 x 0.8 = 1,634 Wh usable. An 800 W furnace running half the time averages 400 W. 1,634 / 400 = about 4.1 hours .
 Illustrations, not predictions: hours of furnace runtime at 80% usable energy Station Stored energy 800 W furnace, running nonstop 800 W furnace, running half the time 490 W furnace, running half the time 
 EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus 1,024 Wh 1.0 hours 2.0 hours 3.3 hours 
 Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 2,042 Wh 2.0 hours 4.1 hours 6.7 hours 
 EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 4,096 Wh 4.1 hours 8.2 hours 13.4 hours 
 800 W is the top of Champion's running range. 490 W is the highest heating draw the DOE study measured after the motor swap. Your furnace may run more or less than half the time. On the coldest nights it runs longer.
 The takeaway: a power station buys you a few warm hours, or one warm night with a large unit. It keeps pipes and people safe while you wait for power or set up a generator. For a multi-day outage, it needs recharging from a generator, a car or solar panels . To test your own mix (furnace plus fridge, lights and phones), add the furnace in the power calculator with the watts from its label.
 How to connect a furnace safely
 Most furnaces are hardwired, with no plug at all. That leaves one safe way to feed them from a generator or station: a listed transfer switch installed on the furnace circuit. OSHA says to never attach a generator to a building's wiring unless a qualified electrician has installed it with a transfer switch.
 Never backfeed the house through a wall or dryer outlet. A double-ended "suicide cord" plugged into an outlet sends generator power into the house wiring. CPSC calls this extremely dangerous : it can electrocute utility workers and neighbors served by the same transformer, and it bypasses some of the home's circuit protection. OSHA adds that it can energize wiring for great distances.
 What a furnace transfer switch does
 A furnace transfer switch sits between the furnace and its normal power. Flip it one way and the furnace runs on the house circuit. Flip it the other way and it runs from whatever you plug into the switch's inlet. Because it can only take power from one source at a time, it cannot backfeed. The EZ Generator Switch FAQ puts it plainly: listed transfer switches do not backfeed.
 Check the listing. The EZ Generator Switch manual lists Model #201 at 15 A, 125 V, conforming to UL Standard 1008 and certified to CSA C22.2 #178.1.
 Hire a qualified installer. The maker sells it as a do-it-yourself kit, but its manual recommends a qualified person do the work and says local codes may apply. OSHA's guidance is a qualified electrician.
 Know your power source's neutral. The EZ switch ships set for bonded-neutral sources and must be converted for floating-neutral ones. Check your generator's or station's manual and tell the installer which you have.
 Read the furnace manual too. Look for any notes on generator or backup power before you buy one.
 Switching over in an outage
 Set up the power source. A generator goes outside, far from the house (see the rules below). A battery power station makes no exhaust, so it can sit near the furnace; follow its manual.
 Run a heavy-duty cord to the switch inlet. CPSC says the cord's wattage rating must exceed what it carries, and it should have all three prongs.
 Start the generator or turn on the station's AC output. 
 Flip the transfer switch to the generator side. The thermostat should call for heat as usual.
 When the power returns, flip the switch back to the house side, then shut down the generator or station.
 Generator for a gas furnace: sizing and safety
 What size generator runs a gas furnace?
 Size for starting watts, not just running watts. Add the running watts of everything you plan to run at once, then add the biggest single starting jump. Using Champion's top figures:
 Using the top of Champion's ranges What you run Running watts Watts at start-up 
 Furnace fan (1/2 HP) alone 800 W 1,600 W 
 Furnace fan plus refrigerator 1,200 W (800 + 400) 2,000 W (1,200 running + 800 extra for one motor starting) 
 Furnace fan, refrigerator and 1/3 HP sump pump 2,000 W (800 + 400 + 800) 2,800 W (2,000 running + 800 extra for one motor starting) 
 Champion lists a refrigerator at 400 W running and 1,200 W starting, and a 1/3 HP sump pump at 800 W running and 1,600 W starting. Each of these motors adds 800 W at start-up, so the table adds 800 W once. A transfer switch for the furnace alone, like the EZ switch, carries only that one circuit. The fridge and sump pump would plug straight into the generator with outdoor-rated cords.
 As an example of fit, Champion's 4500W Electric Start Dual Fuel Inverter lists 4,500 starting watts and 3,500 running watts on gasoline (3,150 running on propane). Champion rates its run time at up to 14 hours on a full 2.3-gallon tank, or 21 hours on a 20 lb propane tank, at 25% load. A quarter of 3,500 W is 875 W, close to one furnace blower at Champion's top figure. Champion also lists its power as under 3% total harmonic distortion.
 Run a generator outdoors only, more than 20 feet from windows, doors and vents. That is CDC's rule for avoiding carbon monoxide poisoning . Never run one inside the house, garage, basement, crawlspace or shed, even with doors and windows open. Most generator incidents reported to CPSC involve carbon monoxide from generators used indoors or in partly enclosed spaces.
 Carbon monoxide alarms. CPSC says to install battery-operated CO alarms, or plug-in alarms with battery backup, certified to UL 2034, IAS 6-96 or CSA 6.19.01. Test the batteries monthly. A generator's own CO shutoff does not replace them.
 Keep it dry. CPSC says to run it under an open, canopy-like cover on a dry surface where water cannot pool, not near openings to the house.
 Refuel cold. Turn it off and let it cool first. Gasoline spilled on hot engine parts can ignite.
 Store fuel outside living areas. CPSC says gasoline, propane and kerosene belong in labeled, non-glass safety containers, away from fuel-burning appliances like a gas water heater in a garage.
 Leave it room. OSHA calls for 3 to 4 feet of clear space on all sides and above a running generator.
 When a furnace is not the answer
 Everything above assumes the heat comes from burning gas, propane or oil, and electricity only runs the fan and controls. Some homes heat with electricity itself.
 Electric furnace or baseboard heat. These make heat from electricity, like a space heater the size of a house. Champion lists a single space heater at 750 to 1,500 W. At 1,500 W, a 1,024 Wh station gives about half an hour (1,024 x 0.8 / 1,500 = 0.55 hours). An electric furnace works the same way for the whole house, so read its data plate before counting on any portable station.
 Heat pump. Champion's chart does not list heat pumps. For a sense of scale, it lists a 2-ton central air conditioner, another outdoor compressor system, at 2,000 to 2,500 W running and 3,500 to 4,500 W starting. Check your heat pump's data plate and plan for a larger generator, a whole-house battery or a different heat source.
 If your heat is electric, or you have no transfer switch yet, plan to heat one room instead. Our guide to staying warm without power covers the warm-room plan. Our indoor propane heater guide covers which heaters are rated for indoor use and how long a tank lasts. Cold rooms also put plumbing at risk, so read how to keep pipes from freezing .

 Questions people ask
 Can a portable power station run a furnace? Yes, if its rated output covers the furnace's running watts and its surge covers the starting watts, and it connects through a transfer switch. Runtime is the limit: hours, not days.
 How long will a portable power station run a gas furnace? Take 80% of its watt-hours and divide by the furnace's average watts. A 2,042 Wh station with an 800 W furnace running half the time gives about 4.1 hours. Running nonstop, about 2 hours. Use your furnace's label for a closer number.
 How do I keep a gas furnace on during a power outage? Have a listed furnace transfer switch installed before winter. In an outage, set up a generator outside (more than 20 feet from openings) or a power station beside the furnace, plug it into the switch's inlet and flip the switch. Keep battery CO alarms working the whole time.
 Can I just plug my furnace into the generator with an extension cord? Only if the furnace has a plug, and most do not; they are hardwired. Never connect a hardwired furnace by plugging the generator into a wall or dryer outlet. That is backfeeding, which CPSC warns can electrocute utility workers.
 Can I run the generator in the garage with the door open? No. CPSC and CDC both say never run a generator in a garage, even with doors and windows open. Carbon monoxide can build to deadly levels and linger for hours after the generator shuts off.

Can a Power Station Run Your Gas Furnace in an Outage? | Outage Authority 
 Charles McQuain · Engineer Published September 30, 2026 · Updated October 7, 2026
 Some links on this page are affiliate links — if you buy something after clicking, we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. Read our full disclosure .
 In February 2021, 246 Texans died in the winter storm, and close to two-thirds of those deaths were hypothermia. A gas furnace is no help in that situation. Without the few hundred watts it needs to light and move air, it sits cold even with gas at the meter. That small electrical load makes a power station sound like the obvious fix: a battery can't heat a house, but it can let the furnace do it.
 It can. But the honest math says hours, not days. There's also a wiring quirk that stops many furnaces from lighting on battery power at all, and almost nobody mentions it until the furnace is clicking and failing at 2 a.m. This page covers both.
 What a gas furnace actually draws
 A gas furnace has four electrical parts, and they don't all run at once. Each time it starts, the inducer fan clears the flue (75W). Then the hot-surface igniter glows for about 37 seconds (400W). Then the gas lights and the control board proves the flame. Once the heat exchanger warms up, the blower starts pushing air through your ducts. Those first three figures come from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's furnace model. The blower is the one that matters, at about 80% of the furnace's electricity, and it depends on which motor you have:
 Furnace electrical loads while heating · LBNL model + NRC field measurement Component Older furnace (PSC blower) Variable-speed (ECM blower) 
 Blower, heating speed 490W 284W 
 Inducer fan 75W 75W 
 Igniter (≈37 sec per start) 400W 400W 
 Controls, standby 5W 9W 
 Running total, burner on ≈565W ≈359W 
 The blower figures are measured, not nameplate. Canada's National Research Council ran two identical test houses side by side and metered both blowers. They moved almost the same air, and the ECM did it on 58% of the power. If your furnace's manual or model sticker says "variable speed" or "ECM," you have the right-hand column. If you're not sure, assume the left. Sizing for the worse case is the whole point.
 None of these loads is hard on an inverter. The igniter's 400W comes on before the blower starts, so the peak is well under 1,000W. Every station on this site has at least 1,500W continuous. Output isn't your constraint. Capacity is. 
 How many hours of heat a battery buys
 A furnace doesn't run all hour. It cycles, and how much of each hour it runs depends on how cold it is outside. The DOE's furnace guideline gives a useful anchor: a house that needs 62,000 Btu/hr at its design low gets sized for an 80,000 Btu/hr furnace. At the coldest night your area is designed for, that furnace runs about 77% of each hour. On a milder outage night, call it half.
 Add the blower and inducer at that share of the hour, standby the rest, and five igniter starts per hour (LBNL's model figure). That gives:
 Older PSC furnace: ~306Wh per hour at half-duty, ~457Wh per hour at design-low duty
 Variable-speed ECM furnace: ~205Wh per hour at half-duty, ~299Wh per hour at design-low duty
 Against real usable capacity, after the 85% inverter haircut this site applies everywhere (the watt-hour calculator explains why):
 Hours of furnace operation per full charge, furnace only · PSC / ECM blower Unit (usable Wh) Mild night (50% duty) Design low (77% duty) 
 Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 (~910Wh) 3.0h / 4.4h 2.0h / 3.0h 
 Bluetti AC180 (~980Wh) 3.2h / 4.8h 2.1h / 3.3h 
 Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 (~1,741Wh) 5.7h / 8.5h 3.8h / 5.8h 
 Bluetti Elite 200 v2 (~1,763Wh) 5.8h / 8.6h 3.9h / 5.9h 
 EcoFlow Delta Pro 3 (~3,482Wh) 11.4h / 17.0h 7.6h / 11.6h 
 That table is the furnace running alone . In a real outage it shares the battery with the fridge, a CPAP, and the router, and the calculator is where you budget all of them together. The takeaway is plain: a 1kWh unit gets you one solid warm-up, not a night of heat. A 2kWh unit gets you through an evening. Only the 4kWh class gets close to keeping a furnace running overnight in real cold.
 Why that's still a great trade
 A few hours sounds disappointing until you compare it to the alternative people actually reach for: a plug-in space heater on the same battery. At 1,500W, a space heater turns every watt into 3.412 Btu/hr of heat, about 5,100 Btu/hr in total. A typical 80,000 Btu/hr furnace at a conservative 80% efficiency puts about 64,000 Btu/hr into the house on roughly 565W of electricity. Per watt-hour of battery, the furnace delivers about 33 times the heat , because the gas does the heating and the battery only runs the fans. A space heater would drain the same Elite 200 v2 in a little over an hour and warm one room. The furnace warms the whole house for most of an evening.
 The grounding problem that keeps furnaces from lighting
 This is the part the "just plug it in" advice skips. Your furnace proves it has a flame using flame rectification . The control board sends a tiny current, usually less than 10 microamps, through the flame itself, and if it sees that current come back, it keeps the gas valve open. That trick depends on a clean reference between neutral and ground. HVAC technicians check that the voltage between the two reads 0.0. At your house that bond is made in the main panel.
 Most portable power stations don't bond neutral to ground . The neutral floats. Mike Sokol, who writes about RV electrical systems, notes that power stations from Jackery, Southwire and Bluetti are built this way. It's a sensible safety choice for a box you might plug a hair dryer into at a campsite. But when a furnace's control board sees a floating neutral, the typical symptom is a furnace that runs its inducer, glows the igniter, lights, fails to prove flame, and shuts the gas off.
 How you connect the furnace decides whether you hit this:
 Through a furnace transfer switch, you don't. A single-circuit furnace switch like Reliance's Easy/Tran keeps the furnace's neutral tied to your panel's neutral bar and only switches the hot wire between utility and battery. The panel's own neutral-ground bond does the job flame rectification needs, and the floating-neutral station is exactly the right kind of source to plug in. Reliance itself warns about the opposite case: a source that's also bonded puts neutral and ground in parallel. Never add a bonding plug to a transfer-switch setup.
 Plugged straight into the station, you might. Some electricians fit a furnace with a cord and plug where local code allows. That puts the furnace on the station's floating neutral with no panel in between. That's the setup where furnaces refuse to light, and where the RV world's fix, a neutral-ground bonding plug in a spare outlet, comes in. If you go that route, let the electrician who wires the cord make the call, not a forum thread.
 Never feed the furnace through a wall outlet
 A male-to-male cord from a power station into a wall or dryer outlet energizes your house wiring and, unless the main breaker is off, the utility lines too. OSHA warns that connecting a generator to a building's wiring without a properly installed transfer switch can energize wiring for great distances, and that's how lineworkers restoring power get electrocuted. A furnace transfer switch's break-before-make relay exists to make that physically impossible. Reliance says to have a licensed electrician or heating contractor install its furnace-side models.
 The Easy/Tran comes in two sizes, the TF151 (1,875W, 15A) and the TF201 (2,500W, 20A). Either clears a residential furnace's running load with lots of room, so match it to your furnace circuit's breaker, not to the furnace.
 The safety upside nobody prices in
 A battery burns nothing. It can sit in the utility closet right next to the furnace, on a short cord, with no exhaust. A gas generator can't. The CPSC says one portable generator produces as much carbon monoxide as hundreds of cars and must never run inside a home or garage. In the 2021 Texas storm, carbon monoxide caused 8% of the deaths. The furnace itself still burns gas and vents exhaust, so keep battery-backed CO alarms on every floor regardless. But the power source is no longer one of your hazards.
 How to run it during an outage
 Warm the house, then stop. Run the furnace until the house is a few degrees above where you'd normally set it, then turn the thermostat down and let the house coast. Restart when it gets uncomfortable. You're spending battery in bursts instead of trickling it away keeping one setpoint.
 Shrink the house. Close doors and supply vents to rooms nobody's using, so the heat you paid battery for stays where people are.
 Keep the fridge on a schedule, not a dedicated circuit. If one battery runs both, alternate them. The CDC says a closed fridge keeps food safely cold for about 4 hours, so it can wait while the furnace runs. A cold house can't.
 Recharge whenever you can. Plug the station back into the wall the moment power returns. In a rolling-blackout event like ERCOT's, the gap between outages is your refill window. The Texas storm prep guide covers that pattern.
 Which battery for furnace backup
 If the furnace is the load that decides your purchase, 2kWh is the floor that makes sense. A 1kWh unit gives you a warm-up, and that's it. Among 2kWh units, the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 is the one we'd buy for this job. It's the cheapest 2kWh capacity we've reviewed, its 2,400W of continuous output is far more than a furnace needs, and it can add an expansion battery later. The Bluetti Elite 200 v2 runs a few minutes longer in the table above and was our pick at its September price of $849. At $1,199 it's $299 more than the Anker, so wait for a sale.
 If you need the furnace to run through a real-cold night without rationing, the EcoFlow Delta Pro 3 is the only portable unit here with the capacity to do it. At that point, also read the whole-house battery backup guide before you spend $2,800. And if what you really want is days of heat, the honest answer is in our generator vs power station guide : a battery is a bridge, and a long freeze is where fuel wins.
 For everything else in the house, the home backup rankings sort every unit here by the same capacity math this page uses.
 Best fit
 Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 2,048Wh · ~3.8–5.7h of furnace · expands to 4kWh 
 The cheapest 2kWh capacity we've reviewed, and for a furnace, watt-hours are runtime. It gets a PSC furnace through an evening of real cold, longer with a variable-speed blower. It's also the only 2kWh unit here that takes an expansion pack: a BP2000 Gen 2 doubles it to 4kWh, the same capacity as the Delta Pro 3 below.
 Check price at Amazon Anker 
 If it's on sale
 Bluetti Elite 200 v2 2,073.6Wh · 2,600W · ~3.9–5.8h of furnace 
 A few minutes more furnace runtime than the Anker and a longer-lived battery, but $1,199 at Bluetti is $299 more for it. Worth buying when a sale brings it near the Anker's price. It can't add an expansion battery, so only if 2kWh is where you'll stay.
 Check price at Bluetti Code AFF5% — 5% off home backup at Bluetti Amazon 
 Overnight in real cold
 EcoFlow Delta Pro 3 4,096Wh · 4,000W · ~7.6–11.4h of furnace 
 The only portable unit here that keeps a PSC furnace running most of a cold night without rationing. Its 240V output means the same battery can feed a multi-circuit transfer switch later.
 Check price at Amazon EcoFlow 
 Frequently asked
 Does a gas furnace work without electricity? + No. The gas gives you the heat, but the furnace can't start or run without electricity. Its inducer fan has to clear the flue before it fires, an electric igniter lights the burner, the control board proves the flame, and the blower pushes the warm air through your ducts. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's furnace model puts the igniter at 400W for about 37 seconds per start and the inducer at 75W. The blower is the big load: 490W for an older PSC motor in a Canadian field measurement, 284W for a variable-speed ECM motor. 
 How long will a power station run a gas furnace? + Hours, not days. An older furnace with a PSC blower uses about 306Wh per hour when it runs half of each hour, and about 457Wh per hour near your area's design low, where a typically oversized furnace runs about three-quarters of the time. That gives a 1kWh-class unit like the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 about 2 to 3 hours of heat, a 2kWh unit like the Bluetti Elite 200 v2 about 4 to 6 hours, and the 4kWh EcoFlow Delta Pro 3 about 7.6 to 11 hours. Newer variable-speed furnaces stretch each figure by roughly half. 
 Why won't my furnace light when it's plugged into a power station? + Most likely the neutral isn't bonded to ground. A furnace proves its flame with a tiny current through the flame itself, called flame rectification. That only works when neutral and ground are tied together, which your main panel does. Most portable power stations leave the neutral floating, so a furnace plugged straight into one can light the igniter, fail to prove flame, and shut the gas off. A transfer switch that keeps the furnace on your house neutral fixes it, because the panel's own bond does the job. 
 Is a power station safer than a gas generator for running a furnace? + For carbon monoxide, yes. A battery burns nothing, so it can sit indoors next to the furnace. The CPSC says a single portable generator produces as much CO as hundreds of cars and must never run inside a home or garage. Carbon monoxide caused 8% of the deaths in Texas's February 2021 winter storm. Either way, the furnace itself still burns gas and vents exhaust, so keep battery-backed CO alarms working through any outage. 
 Can I plug a power station into a wall outlet to power the furnace circuit? + No. A male-to-male cord into a wall or dryer outlet backfeeds your house wiring, and potentially the utility lines, with nothing to stop it. OSHA warns that connecting a generator to a building's wiring without a properly installed transfer switch can energize wiring systems for great distances, which is how lineworkers restoring power get electrocuted. A furnace transfer switch exists precisely to make that impossible.

 Quick Answer 
 Yes, a properly sized portable power station can run many residential gas furnaces during a power outage. Even though the furnace produces heat by burning natural gas or propane, it still needs electricity for the blower motor, inducer motor, ignition system, control board, gas valve, and safety controls.
 For a typical 120V forced-air gas furnace, the two numbers that matter most are the furnace's actual running watts and its highest startup demand . A rough planning range of several hundred watts is useful when shopping, but it should not replace checking or measuring your own furnace.
 A 1,200W-class power station can be appropriate for a furnace whose measured electrical demand stays comfortably within that output limit. A 2,400W-class unit provides much more headroom for higher blower loads, startup demand, longer outages, or a few additional essentials. Hardwired furnaces require a safe, code-compliant connection method; do not backfeed a wall outlet or improvise a connection to your electrical panel.
 Will a Gas Furnace Work During a Power Outage?
 Usually not. A modern gas furnace needs both fuel and electricity.
 Natural gas or propane supplies the heat, but electricity operates the parts that allow the furnace to start, move air, monitor the flame, and shut itself down safely. Depending on the furnace, those electrical loads can include:
 Circulating blower motor
 Draft inducer motor
 Electronic ignition system
 Furnace control board
 Gas valve and safety controls
 Thermostat or connected HVAC controls
 Condensate equipment on some high-efficiency installations
 The blower is often one of the largest electrical loads. Lennox describes the furnace blower motor as the electric motor responsible for moving conditioned air through the duct system. Lennox: HVAC Blower Motor .
 This is why a house can still have natural gas service during a blackout while the furnace remains completely unusable.
 Important distinction: A gas furnace is very different from an electric furnace. A typical portable 120V battery power station may be capable of supporting the electrical components of a gas furnace. An electric resistance furnace can require many thousands of watts and commonly uses 240V service, putting it in an entirely different backup power category.
 How Many Watts Does a Gas Furnace Use?
 There is no single correct "furnace wattage." A small modern furnace with an efficient variable-speed ECM blower may draw dramatically less power at a low airflow setting than an older furnace with a conventional blower running at high speed.
 As an initial shopping estimate, several hundred watts is reasonable for many forced-air gas furnaces. However, published estimates vary widely, and your actual furnace should determine the final power station size.

 UDPOWER sizing guide 
 Why Furnace Blower Watts Vary So Much
 Blower wattage is affected by more than the motor label. Motor design, commanded airflow, duct resistance, filter condition, blower speed and system static pressure all influence electrical demand.
 Current Lennox engineering data for a variable-speed ECM furnace family illustrates this clearly: published blower input watts change substantially as airflow settings and external static pressure change. That means a wattage number from another homeowner's furnace is not necessarily a reliable prediction for yours. View Lennox engineering data .
 A useful backup-power lesson: If you clean or replace a badly restricted filter and correct airflow problems, you are not merely improving comfort. On some systems, you may also change the electrical demand of the blower. Your furnace's real-world battery runtime can therefore differ from a simple internet wattage estimate.
 6 Things to Check Before Buying a Furnace Battery Backup
 1. Is the Furnace 120V?
 Many residential forced-air gas furnaces in the U.S. operate from a 120V branch circuit. Confirm the actual electrical requirements on your furnace documentation or equipment label.
 This matters because portable power stations such as the UDPOWER S1200 and S2400 provide U.S.-standard 120V AC output. They are not replacements for 240V whole-home electrical service.
 2. What Is the Actual Running Load?
 This number determines how heavily the inverter will be loaded and is the foundation of your runtime calculation.
 3. What Happens When the Blower or Inducer Starts?
 Motors can demand more power while starting than while operating normally. A power station that looks large enough based only on steady running watts can still shut down if the startup demand exceeds what its inverter can support.
 4. Is the Furnace Plug-Connected or Hardwired?
 This can be more important than wattage.
 If the furnace has been installed with an approved cord-and-plug arrangement, powering it from a power station may be relatively straightforward when permitted by the equipment instructions and local electrical requirements.
 A hardwired furnace is different. You should not cut wires, fabricate a plug, backfeed an outlet, or improvise a panel connection during a blackout.
 5. Does the Furnace Operate Correctly on the Backup Source?
 A furnace contains more than a blower. Modern ignition and flame-sensing electronics can make some systems more sensitive to power-source characteristics and grounding arrangements than an ordinary lamp or phone charger.
 6. How Long Do You Actually Need Heat?
 An inverter rating answers, "Can it run the load?" Battery capacity answers, "For approximately how long?" You need both numbers.
 How to Find Your Furnace's Real Power Demand
 The best furnace backup calculation uses the entire furnace's actual electrical consumption rather than a generic blower watt number.
 If Your Furnace Has an Approved Plug Connection
 Check the furnace manual and equipment label for voltage and electrical requirements.
 Use a properly rated power meter if the installation allows one to be safely placed between the receptacle and furnace.
 Start a normal heating cycle.
 Observe the furnace during ignition, inducer operation and blower startup.
 Record the normal operating watts and the highest demand your meter can reliably capture.
 Repeat the observation through several cycles rather than relying on a few seconds of data.
 If Your Furnace Is Hardwired
 Do not open energized wiring or attempt DIY measurements inside a furnace disconnect or electrical panel just to obtain a wattage number. Ask an HVAC technician or electrician to verify the electrical load and, if necessary, test it with appropriate equipment.
 Do not confuse breaker size with actual furnace wattage. A furnace being connected to a 15A circuit does not mean it continuously consumes 15A × 120V = 1,800W. The circuit is sized to safely supply the equipment; it is not a real-time energy meter.
 How Long Will a Battery Run a Gas Furnace?
 Once you know the approximate running watts, battery runtime becomes much easier to estimate. UDPOWER's practical planning method uses about 90% of nominal capacity when making a first-pass runtime estimate:
 Estimated runtime = Battery capacity (Wh) × 0.90 ÷ Furnace load (W) 
 This is a planning estimate rather than a guarantee. Real runtime changes with inverter efficiency, temperature, furnace cycling, battery condition, airflow, auxiliary loads and the exact operating state of the HVAC system.
 The following examples use: UDPOWER S1200 — 1,190Wh and UDPOWER S2400 — 2,083Wh .

 How Much Battery Capacity Do You Need Overnight?
 This is where many furnace backup guides become misleading.
 A furnace that consumes 500W while heating does not necessarily consume 500W for eight straight hours. Once the home reaches the thermostat setpoint, the burner and blower shut down. The percentage of the night spent actively heating is called the duty cycle .
 For example, a 500W furnace operating 50% of an eight-hour night runs for about four total hours. At a 90% planning efficiency, that calls for roughly:

 This table explains why outside temperature matters so much. The same furnace can last comfortably through a mild fall outage yet drain the same battery much faster during a severe cold snap.
 Other factors that can raise the overnight duty cycle include:
 Poor insulation or significant air leakage
 Very low outdoor temperatures
 A high thermostat setting
 Undersized heating equipment
 Open exterior doors
 Restricted airflow
 Heating rooms that do not need to remain fully conditioned during the outage
 Better planning strategy: Instead of asking only "How long will a 1,000Wh battery run my furnace?", determine your furnace's measured watts and how often it typically runs on a cold night. Those two numbers produce a much more useful answer.

 For furnace backup, inverter output should be selected first. Battery capacity comes second. There is little benefit in buying a large battery if its inverter cannot reliably start the furnace.

 The correct connection depends on how the furnace was installed. Do not assume that because the power station has an AC receptacle, every furnace can simply be plugged into it.
 Scenario 1: Furnace Already Uses an Approved Plug
 If your furnace has a manufacturer- and code-compliant cord-and-plug connection, using a suitable battery power source may be comparatively simple. Confirm:
 The furnace is designed for 120V AC power.
 The power station provides enough running output.
 The starting demand is within supported limits.
 The cord, receptacle and installation comply with the furnace manufacturer's requirements.
 The furnace completes several normal heating cycles during a test.
 Scenario 2: Furnace Is Hardwired
 A hardwired furnace requires a properly designed means of transferring it from utility power to backup power. This is not a situation for improvised cords.
 A licensed electrician can determine whether a suitable furnace transfer device, approved disconnect arrangement, transfer switch or other code-compliant solution is appropriate for your installation.
 Never backfeed the house. Do not connect a portable power station or generator to a wall receptacle in an attempt to energize household wiring. Improper backfeeding can create shock and fire hazards and can endanger utility workers. The Electrical Safety Foundation International also advises using an appropriate transfer method rather than connecting backup sources improperly to home wiring.
 Why Grounding and Neutral Compatibility Can Matter
 If the blower starts on battery power but the furnace refuses to ignite, repeatedly locks out, or reports a flame-related fault, the problem is not automatically "not enough watts."
 Modern furnaces use electronic ignition and flame-safety circuits. Some HVAC equipment can be sensitive to correct line polarity, grounding and the electrical system's neutral/ground arrangement.
 Portable power sources can use different neutral configurations depending on their design. Generac's electrical guidance, for example, distinguishes between bonded-neutral and floating-neutral power sources. Generac: Bonded vs. Floating Neutral .
 Do not solve a furnace ignition problem by installing a homemade neutral-ground bonding adapter. If the furnace behaves differently on backup power, stop and have a qualified electrician or HVAC technician determine the cause and the correct code-compliant solution for that specific installation.
 This is also why the phrase "pure sine wave" should not be treated as a complete furnace compatibility guarantee. Waveform quality matters, but voltage, frequency, grounding, connection method, output capacity and the furnace's own electronics matter too.
 What Not to Do During a Furnace Power Outage
 Do Not Backfeed a Wall Outlet
 A male-to-male cord or any improvised method of energizing household wiring through a receptacle is unsafe.
 Do Not Assume a 15A Breaker Means the Furnace Uses 1,800W
 Breaker capacity and actual operating demand are different measurements.
 Do Not Put the Power Station Inside the Furnace Cabinet
 Keep the unit in a dry, ventilated location and follow the clearances and operating instructions in its manual. Do not block cooling openings or place battery equipment against hot furnace surfaces.
 Do Not Run a Large Electric Space Heater Unless You Have Planned for It
 A 1,500W resistance heater can consume 1.5kWh in only one hour of continuous operation. If your goal is to stretch limited battery capacity through a winter blackout, using electricity to operate the controls and blower of an existing gas furnace can be far more practical than trying to produce the heat itself with a high-watt electric heater.
 Do Not Wait for the Blizzard to Test the Setup
 A furnace that works normally on utility power may reveal an installation, connection or compatibility problem when moved to backup power. The safest time to discover that problem is before the outage.

 A Practical Winter Outage Plan
 Buying the battery is only one part of keeping a house warm during an outage. A better approach is to prepare the entire heating plan before winter.
 Before the Storm
 Confirm the furnace voltage and electrical connection type.
 Determine actual operating wattage if possible.
 Have a professional prepare a compliant backup connection if the furnace is hardwired.
 Fully charge the power station.

 Replace or clean the furnace filter if needed.
 Decide which other appliances are truly essential.
 Keep flashlights, charging cables and backup lighting accessible.
 When the Power Goes Out
 Check the power station's state of charge.
 Run the furnace using only the previously tested, safe connection method.
 Keep unnecessary high-watt appliances off.
 Close exterior doors quickly and minimize heat loss.
 Consider temporarily lowering the thermostat to reduce furnace duty cycle.
 Monitor remaining battery percentage rather than assuming the initial runtime estimate will be exact.
 Prioritize the Right Loads
 During a winter outage, the best use of stored energy is usually not "run everything normally." A more resilient load list might look like:
 Gas furnace — protects comfort and, in severe cold, may help reduce pipe-freezing risk.
 Essential medical equipment — when applicable.
 Refrigerator or freezer — run strategically rather than automatically adding every appliance.
 Internet equipment and phones — relatively small loads that preserve communications.
 LED lighting — low energy cost compared with heating appliances.

 Gas Furnace Battery Backup FAQs
 Can a power station run a gas furnace?
 Yes. Many 120V gas furnaces can operate from a properly sized portable power station because the battery is powering the blower, inducer, ignition and controls rather than creating the heat itself. You still need to verify running watts, startup demand, electrical connection and furnace compatibility.
 Will a gas furnace work without electricity?
 Normally, no. Even though natural gas or propane provides the heat, a modern forced-air furnace depends on electrically powered controls, ignition and air-moving equipment.
 How many watts does a furnace blower use?
 There is no universal number. Blower wattage varies with motor type, airflow, blower speed, duct resistance and static pressure. Modern ECM blowers can use comparatively little power at lower airflow settings and much more as airflow demand rises. For battery sizing, measuring the complete furnace is more useful than relying on an average blower-watt figure.
 What size battery backup do I need for a gas furnace?
 Choose enough inverter output to comfortably support both normal operation and startup demand, then calculate battery capacity from the furnace's running watts, desired heating time and expected duty cycle. A 1,200W-class station may work for a verified lower-load furnace; a 2,400W-class station provides more output margin and is generally more suitable when additional essential loads are involved.
 How long will a 1,000Wh battery run a gas furnace?
 It depends on furnace wattage. Using a 90% planning factor gives about 900Wh of usable energy for a quick estimate. At 300W, that is about 3 hours of continuous operation; at 500W, about 1.8 hours; at 700W, about 1.3 hours. Because a furnace normally cycles, actual elapsed time can be longer.
 Can the UDPOWER S1200 run my gas furnace?
 It can run a compatible furnace whose electrical demand fits within the S1200's specifications. The S1200 has a 1,200W rated pure sine wave AC output and 1,190Wh battery capacity. Do not decide based on the words "gas furnace" alone; verify the electrical load of your exact unit.
 Is the UDPOWER S2400 better for furnace backup?
 The S2400 provides 2,400W rated AC output and 2,083Wh capacity, giving more output headroom and longer runtime than the S1200. It is particularly useful when the furnace has a higher electrical demand or you intend to operate a few additional essential devices.
 Can I simply plug my furnace into a portable power station?
 Only if the furnace already has an approved cord-and-plug connection and the installation, furnace instructions and local electrical requirements permit it. Many furnaces are hardwired. A hardwired furnace needs a properly designed backup-power connection rather than an improvised cord.
 Can I connect a power station to my home's transfer switch?
 That depends on the equipment and electrical design. UDPOWER states that the S2400 should not be directly connected to a home transfer switch unless the arrangement has been reviewed and installed by a licensed electrician. It supplies U.S.-standard 120V AC and should never be used to backfeed household wiring.
 Can I use a power station's UPS function for my furnace?
 A fast UPS transfer time can be useful, but it does not guarantee that every furnace will operate correctly. The furnace still needs compatible voltage, adequate output capacity, an appropriate grounding arrangement and a safe electrical connection. Test the actual setup before relying on it for a winter emergency.
 Why does my furnace blower work on battery power but the burner will not stay lit?
 Do not automatically assume the battery is too small. Ignition and flame-sensing systems can be affected by wiring polarity, grounding or the neutral arrangement of the power source. Stop repeated troubleshooting if the furnace faults or locks out and have an HVAC technician or electrician evaluate the system. Do not improvise a bonding adapter.
 Can a portable power station run an electric furnace?
 A typical portable 120V power station is generally not an appropriate substitute for the high-power 240V supply used by many electric resistance furnaces. Gas-furnace backup is much more practical because the battery powers the electrical components while natural gas or propane supplies the heat.
 Can I run my furnace and refrigerator from the same power station?
 Possibly. Add the simultaneous running loads and consider the startup behavior of both motor-driven appliances. The combined demand must stay within the power station's supported output, and both appliances will reduce battery runtime. A higher-output, higher-capacity model such as the S2400 offers more margin for this type of backup plan.
 Is a space heater a good alternative during a power outage?
 Usually not if your goal is to maximize battery runtime. Many portable electric heaters draw around 1,500W at their highest setting and convert battery energy directly into heat. If a functioning gas furnace can be safely powered, using the battery for the furnace's blower and controls can make much better use of limited stored electricity.
 Should a furnace backup power station have pure sine wave output?
 Pure sine wave AC is the appropriate choice for modern furnaces containing motors and electronic controls. Both the UDPOWER S1200 and S2400 provide pure sine wave AC output. Waveform alone, however, does not replace checking voltage, wattage, startup demand, grounding and the connection method.

 Can a Portable Power Station Run a Gas Furnace During an Outage?
 Aug 4, 2026 
 By STOREOUPES
 Yes, a portable power station can run many gas furnaces during an outage, but only when its AC output, surge capability, battery capacity, grounding arrangement, and connection method are compatible with the specific furnace. A gas furnace burns fuel for heat, yet its blower motor, ignition system, control board, inducer fan, and safety controls still need electricity. Do not choose a power station from the furnace's heating rating or from a generic online wattage estimate. Start with the furnace nameplate, manual, and manufacturer guidance.
 The practical decision has two parts: the power station must handle the furnace's momentary startup demand, and it must store enough energy to support the furnace through the expected outage. The calculations below provide a planning method, not a guarantee for every installation.
 Why a Gas Furnace Needs Electricity
 A modern gas furnace is not a passive heater. Its control board verifies safe operating conditions, an inducer fan establishes draft, an igniter starts combustion, and a blower distributes heated air. Thermostats, condensate equipment, dampers, and other accessories may add electrical demand. If any required component loses power, the furnace generally cannot complete its normal heating cycle.
 Electrical demand also changes during a cycle. A motor may draw more power for a brief moment when it starts than it uses after reaching normal speed. The furnace then cycles on and off according to thermostat settings, outdoor temperature, insulation, and heat loss. That is why a single “furnace wattage” number cannot reliably predict either compatibility or runtime.
 Check Running and Startup Power
 First, locate the furnace nameplate and manual. Record voltage, amperage, motor ratings, and any stated minimum circuit or startup requirements. If the furnace manufacturer provides a backup-power procedure, follow it. A qualified HVAC or electrical professional can measure actual demand when the documentation is incomplete.
 For a basic estimate, watts equal volts multiplied by amps. For example, a 120-volt load drawing 6 amps represents about 720 watts while operating. This arithmetic is only a starting point: motors and power-factor effects can make actual behavior more complicated, and the startup peak may be higher than the steady draw.
 Compare three items before use:
 Continuous AC output: it must exceed the combined running demand of the furnace and every other connected load.
 Startup demand: the power station must tolerate the motor's brief starting requirement without shutting down.
 Output compatibility: voltage, frequency, receptacles, grounding behavior, and any manufacturer requirements must suit the installation.
 Leave operating margin rather than planning to hold an inverter at its maximum rating. Also account for a condensate pump, powered thermostat, zone equipment, or other components that must operate with the furnace.
 Estimate Battery Runtime
 Output power is measured in watts, while stored energy is measured in watt-hours. Runtime depends primarily on energy capacity and average load, not merely on the inverter's maximum watt rating. A useful planning formula is:
 Estimated runtime in hours = battery capacity in Wh × planning efficiency ÷ average load in W 
 Suppose a power station stores 2,048Wh. Using an illustrative 85% planning factor leaves about 1,741Wh for the estimate. If the furnace and required controls averaged 700W while actively running, the continuous-load estimate would be about 2.5 hours. A cycling furnace may span a longer clock period because it does not run every minute, while very cold weather may increase its duty cycle. Conversion losses, temperature, battery condition, and accessory loads can reduce the result.
 Do not turn this example into a promised runtime. A better method is to measure or document the actual load, estimate how many minutes per hour the furnace operates under expected conditions, and include a reserve. During a severe winter outage, indoor heat loss and furnace cycling can differ substantially from a mild-day test.
 Connection, Grounding, and Safety
 The connection method is often the decisive issue. Many furnaces are hardwired rather than fitted with an ordinary plug. Do not improvise a cord, backfeed a household circuit, bypass furnace safety controls, or attempt a panel modification from a generic tutorial. Any fixed wiring, transfer equipment, or conversion should be evaluated and installed by a qualified professional in accordance with the furnace instructions and local requirements.
 Some heating equipment may also be sensitive to grounding or neutral configuration. A furnace that works from utility power may display a fault when connected to an incompatible source. Ask the furnace manufacturer or a qualified professional what the equipment requires, and confirm that the proposed power station and connection method meet it.
 Place the power station in a dry, stable, ventilated location within its specified operating conditions. Keep vents clear, protect cables from damage, and keep the unit away from furnace heat, condensate, snow, and water. A battery power station produces no combustion exhaust, but it still must be used according to its manual. Never place a fuel-burning generator indoors as a substitute.
 Choose a Practical Capacity
 Choose capacity around the outage plan, not around the furnace alone. For short heating intervals, calculate one or two expected cycles plus a safety reserve. For overnight planning, estimate the furnace duty cycle across the coldest likely period. If the same power station will also support a refrigerator, lights, communications, or medical equipment, calculate simultaneous watts and total watt-hours for every priority load.
 A sensible plan separates loads into three groups:
 Essential: furnace controls and blower, required health equipment, and critical communications.
 Scheduled: refrigerator, freezer, device charging, and lights that can operate at different times.
 Deferred: resistance heaters, cooking appliances, and other high-demand devices that can quickly consume the energy reserve.
 Load scheduling can be as useful as buying more capacity. Avoid running a high-watt appliance while the blower starts, and monitor the power station's display instead of assuming the original estimate remains accurate.
 A Local OUPES Option
 For a furnace whose verified electrical requirements fit within its limits, the OUPES Mega 2 Pro Portable Power Station provides 2,500W of rated AC output and 2,048Wh of stored capacity. Those figures create useful planning room for many household backup scenarios, but they do not establish compatibility with a particular furnace. The nameplate, startup behavior, grounding requirements, connection method, and combined load still control the decision.
 The product data also lists up to 2,100W of solar input. That input rating is not a promise of constant solar production, and the power station is sold here as a standalone unit without a solar panel. Actual solar replenishment depends on connected panels, sunlight, angle, shading, weather, and system limits. In a winter outage, reliable access to utility charging before the event may be more predictable than assuming daily solar recovery.
 Pre-Outage Checklist
 Photograph the furnace nameplate and save the manual.
 Confirm continuous demand, startup demand, voltage, frequency, grounding, and connection requirements.
 Have any fixed connection or transfer equipment handled by a qualified professional.
 Test the approved setup before severe weather while utility power and professional help are available.
 Calculate essential watt-hours, add a reserve, and plan which secondary loads will be scheduled.
 Fully charge the power station before forecast winter storms and store it within specified conditions.
 During use, monitor remaining charge, load, temperature, cables, and furnace behavior.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 How many watts does a gas furnace use?
 There is no dependable universal figure. Blower size, inducer motor, accessories, voltage, design, and operating stage all matter. Read the furnace nameplate and manual, then obtain actual measurements or professional guidance when needed. Plan for both steady demand and the brief startup requirement rather than selecting from an online average.
 Will a 2,000Wh battery run a furnace all night?
 It might cover part or all of an overnight period, but capacity alone cannot answer the question. Runtime depends on active wattage, cycling frequency, inverter losses, temperature, battery condition, and other loads. Calculate usable watt-hours against the furnace's measured average demand and retain a reserve for colder-than-expected conditions.
 Can I plug a hardwired furnace directly into a power station?
 Not unless the furnace manufacturer and a qualified professional approve a compliant connection method. Do not add a makeshift plug, backfeed wiring, or bypass safety equipment. Fixed wiring, transfer equipment, neutral configuration, and grounding require installation-specific review under applicable instructions and local requirements.
 Should I run a space heater from the same power station?
 Usually that would consume the battery much faster and could leave less output margin for the furnace motor. Resistance heaters are high, sustained loads. Compare the combined wattage with the inverter rating and the total watt-hours with your outage plan; prioritize the furnace and other essential loads when energy is limited.
 Can solar panels recharge the battery during a winter outage?
 Solar can extend a backup plan, but winter output varies with daylight, cloud cover, panel angle, shade, snow, and temperature. A product's solar-input rating is a maximum input specification, not guaranteed daily energy. Base the plan on realistic local conditions and treat favorable solar production as variable.
 What should I test before the next outage?
 After the connection method has been professionally approved, test furnace startup, a full heating cycle, thermostat response, error codes, cable temperature, and the power station's displayed load. Record energy used over a representative period. Repeat the check periodically and after changes to the furnace or backup equipment.
 Conclusion
 A portable power station can be a practical gas-furnace backup when its continuous output, startup handling, capacity, grounding behavior, and approved connection method all match the real installation. Verify the furnace data first, calculate watt-hours with losses and cycling in mind, and leave fixed electrical work to a qualified professional. That disciplined approach is more reliable than choosing a battery from a generic furnace wattage estimate.

 Why a gas furnace stops working in an outage
 When the grid goes down, the gas still flows, but the furnace will not light or move air. Its electric parts control everything: the inducer fan clears the flue, the igniter lights the burner, the control board runs the sequence, and the blower pushes warm air through your ducts.
 The good news is that these parts usually need far less power than an electric heater. That puts many furnaces within reach of a portable power station, which has no exhaust and can sit indoors near the furnace.
 Find your furnace's real power draw
 Do not guess. Furnace loads vary a lot by model, blower size, and motor type. Start with the nameplate on the furnace, usually inside the front panel. It lists volts and amps for the unit or the blower motor. Volts times amps gives a rough upper estimate in watts.
 A better number comes from a measurement. Because many furnaces are hardwired, a plug-in watt meter will not work unless your furnace already has a cord and plug. An electrician can measure the running draw with a clamp meter while the furnace goes through a full heating cycle.
 Motors pull extra power for a moment when they start. Ask for the startup reading too, or check that the power station's surge rating leaves plenty of room above your running number.
 Nameplate volts and amps for the furnace or blower

 Whether your blower has more than one speed setting
 Do the runtime math
 Your furnace does not run nonstop. It cycles on and off with the thermostat, and colder weather means longer cycles. That cycling is what stretches a battery.
 For example, if your furnace measures 400 watts while running and runs about half of each hour, it uses about 200 watt-hours per hour. To estimate runtime, divide the watt-hour capacity on your power station's spec sheet by that hourly use, and expect somewhat less in practice because converting battery power to AC loses some energy. Use your own measured number, and check the maker's runtime chart at your load.
 To stretch runtime, lower the thermostat a few degrees, close doors to rooms you are not using, and plan a way to recharge, such as solar panels or a car charger if the unit supports them.
 Check the output type and power quality
 Furnace control boards and modern blower motors can be picky about power. Look for a spec sheet that says pure sine wave output. On a modified sine wave inverter, some furnaces may fault, run rough, or refuse to light.
 Some furnace controls may also need correct polarity and a ground before they ignite, and a portable source can upset that. This is one more reason to have an electrician set up and test the connection before you need it.
 Connect it safely
 Most gas furnaces are wired directly into a circuit with a service switch, so there is no plug to move to a power station. Do not cut wires, make your own cords, or back-feed a circuit. A licensed electrician can add a safe connection, such as a cord-and-plug setup at the furnace or a transfer switch, and tell you what outlet type and cord your setup needs.
 Test the whole setup on a mild day. Run a full heating cycle on the power station, watch for error codes, and note how fast the battery drops.
 If you also own a generator, never run it indoors, in a garage, or near windows, because of carbon monoxide. Keep working carbon monoxide alarms in your home either way, since the furnace itself burns gas.

The good news is that it needs far less power than electric heat: the gas does the heating, the electricity only moves air. Running it on a power station is one of the most efficient ways to heat a whole house in an outage.
 Older blowers (PSC motors) often draw 400–800 W.
 Newer variable-speed (ECM) blowers can draw much less at low speed, sometimes under 200 W.
 The furnace cycles with the thermostat, so its average over an hour depends on how cold it is outside and how warm you keep the house.
 Measure your own furnace if you can: an electrician can clamp a meter on its supply, or you can read the blower motor's amps on its label and multiply by 120.
 How to connect it safely
 Most furnaces are wired straight into a circuit with a service switch, not plugged in. The safe options, installed by a licensed electrician, are:
 a furnace transfer switch with an inlet you plug the station into, or
 a manual transfer switch or inlet for a few essential circuits, including the furnace.
 Never backfeed your house by plugging a station into a wall outlet with a double-ended cord. It can electrocute utility workers and start fires.
 If the furnace won't light on the power station
 Furnace flame sensors need correct polarity and, in many cases, a neutral connected to ground. Some power stations have a "floating" neutral, and a furnace on one may try to ignite, then shut down. If that happens, ask an HVAC technician or electrician to check the connection. Don't bypass any furnace safety control.
 Stretch the battery
 Lower the thermostat a few degrees: fewer cycles means proportionally more hours.
 Close off rooms you aren't using and keep curtains closed at night.
 Add solar or a car charger for long outages, and keep the station indoors, since batteries lose capacity in the cold. An electric blanket at night uses far less.
 Frequently asked questions
 What size power station do I need for a gas furnace? + At least 1,000 W of continuous output for most furnaces, and 2,000 Wh or more of capacity for about 6 hours of heating at a typical 300 W average. Variable-speed blowers use less, older PSC blowers more.
 Can I plug my furnace into a power station? + Only after an electrician installs a transfer switch or inlet. Most furnaces are hard-wired. Never backfeed your house through a wall outlet.
 Is it safe to run a gas furnace during a power outage? + Yes, when it's powered properly and its flue and safety controls work normally. A power station runs indoors with no exhaust, unlike a gas generator, which must stay outside, far from doors and windows. Keep a working carbon monoxide alarm, as you always should with gas appliances.

Can a Power Station Run a Gas Furnace? Watts & Runtime | UTrendCo 
 Illustration: not a specific product. 
 On this page 
 Why does a gas furnace stop working when the power goes out? 
 How many watts does a gas furnace use? 
 What size power station do you need for a furnace? 
 How long will a power station run a gas furnace? 
 Which power stations can start and run a furnace? 
 How do you safely connect a power station to a furnace? 
 How can you make the battery last longer? 
 FAQ 
 Sources 
 Yes, if it has pure sine wave output, enough surge to start the blower, and a safe connection. How many watts a gas furnace uses, how long 1,000 to 4,000Wh stations run it, and how to hook one up safely.
 Short answer: yes, a portable power station can run most 120V gas furnaces during an outage, as long as it has pure sine wave output, enough surge power to start the blower, and a safe, code-compliant connection. The gas makes the heat, but the blower, draft inducer, igniter and control board all need electricity. A typical furnace draws roughly 300 to 800 watts while it runs, so a 2,000Wh station keeps it going for about 3.5 hours of nonstop blower time, or around 7 hours when the furnace cycles on and off.
 Why does a gas furnace stop working when the power goes out?
 A modern forced-air gas furnace can't light or move heat without electricity. Every heating cycle follows the same sequence: the thermostat calls for heat, the control board starts the draft inducer fan to clear the exhaust, a hot surface igniter or spark lights the burners, a flame sensor confirms the flame, and then the blower pushes warm air through your ducts. If any of those steps loses power, the gas valve stays shut for safety.
 That's good news for battery backup. You don't need to replace the heat, only the few hundred watts that run the fans and controls. That's a far easier job than running a 1,500W space heater, which empties a 1,000Wh station in about 34 minutes (see our space heater runtime guide ).
 How many watts does a gas furnace use?
 Most of the power goes to the blower motor. Older furnaces use a PSC (permanent split capacitor) blower, which commonly draws about 300 to 700 watts. Newer furnaces often use an ECM (electronically commutated, variable-speed) blower that can run below 100 watts at low speed and a few hundred watts at high speed.
 Furnace part Typical draw When it runs 
 Control board and 24V transformer 5 to 15W Always 
 Draft inducer fan 50 to 150W Whole burn cycle 
 Hot surface igniter 300 to 500W 15 to 60 seconds per start 
 Blower, PSC motor 300 to 700W Most of the burn cycle 
 Blower, ECM motor 75 to 500W Most of the burn cycle, speed varies 
 Honda's generator sizing guide lists a 1/3-horsepower furnace fan at about 700 running watts and 1,400 starting watts, and a 1/2-horsepower furnace fan at about 875 running watts and 2,350 starting watts. Those are cautious planning figures for older motors; many furnaces measure lower.
 The igniter usually shuts off before the blower starts, so the two biggest loads rarely overlap. Your real peak is the larger of "inducer plus igniter" or "inducer plus blower starting up."
 How to find your furnace's real number
 Read the nameplate. It's usually inside the front panel and lists volts and amps. Volts times amps gives a worst-case figure (for example, 120V × 7A = 840W), which usually overstates the running load.
 Check the blower motor label for its horsepower and whether it's PSC or ECM.
 Measure it. Furnaces are usually hardwired, so a plug-in watt meter won't work, but an electrician can read the running draw with a clamp meter during a full heating cycle.
 What size power station do you need for a furnace?
 Check three numbers on the power station's spec sheet, in this order:
 Output waveform: pure sine wave. Furnace control boards, flame sensing and ECM motors can fault, buzz or lock out on modified sine wave power. Most name-brand lithium power stations list pure sine wave output, but confirm it on the spec sheet, especially on cheaper inverters.
 Surge (peak) rating above the blower's starting watts. A 1/2-hp PSC blower may need about 2,350W for a split second; an ECM blower needs far less. A station with 3,000W or more of surge covers nearly any residential furnace.
 Capacity in watt-hours for runtime. This decides how many hours of heat you get.
 For most homes, a station with at least 1,800W continuous output, 3,000W or more of surge, and 2,000Wh or more of capacity is the practical starting point for overnight furnace backup.
 How long will a power station run a gas furnace?
 Use the same formula we use across the site:
 Runtime (hours) = Capacity (Wh) × 0.85 ÷ Furnace watts 
 The 0.85 covers inverter and conversion losses. A furnace also doesn't run nonstop: it cycles on and off with the thermostat. On a cold night it might run about half of each hour, which roughly doubles the runtime. The table shows both cases.
 Power station capacity Efficient ECM furnace (250W) Typical PSC furnace (500W) Large 1/2-hp blower (875W) 
 1,000Wh 3.4 h nonstop / 6.8 h cycling 1.7 h / 3.4 h 1.0 h / 1.9 h 
 2,000Wh 6.8 h / 13.6 h 3.4 h / 6.8 h 1.9 h / 3.9 h 
 3,000Wh 10.2 h / 20.4 h 5.1 h / 10.2 h 2.9 h / 5.8 h 
 4,000Wh 13.6 h / 27.2 h 6.8 h / 13.6 h 3.9 h / 7.8 h 
 A 2,000Wh power station runs a typical 500W furnace for about 3.4 hours of continuous blower time, or roughly 6.8 hours if the furnace runs half of each hour. A furnace with an efficient ECM blower can get through a whole night on the same battery.
 Which power stations can start and run a furnace?
 Here's how popular models compare, using manufacturer-published capacity, continuous output and surge ratings, and a 500W furnace load.
 Power station Capacity Continuous / surge Covers a 2,350W start? 500W furnace, nonstop / cycling 
 EcoFlow Delta 3 1,024Wh 1,800W / 3,600W Yes 1.7 h / 3.5 h 
 Anker Solix C1000 1,056Wh 1,800W / 2,400W Barely 1.8 h / 3.6 h 
 Jackery Explorer 1000 Plus 1,264Wh 2,000W / 4,000W Yes 2.1 h / 4.3 h 
 Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 2,042Wh 2,200W / 4,400W Yes 3.5 h / 6.9 h 
 Anker Solix C2000 Gen 2 2,048Wh 2,400W / 4,000W Yes 3.5 h / 7.0 h 
 Jackery HomePower 3000 3,072Wh 3,600W / 7,200W Yes 5.2 h / 10.4 h 
 EcoFlow Delta Pro 3 4,096Wh 4,000W / 8,000W Yes 7.0 h / 13.9 h 
 The 1kWh class can start most furnaces but only buys a few hours. For a full winter night, a 2kWh station is the realistic minimum, and a 3 to 4kWh unit or an expandable system is better if outages in your area last more than a day. Our 2000Wh runtime guide shows what else fits in that budget, and the best home backup power stations list compares the bigger units.
 How do you safely connect a power station to a furnace?
 This is the part that matters most. Most furnaces are hardwired to their own circuit with a service switch, not plugged into an outlet. There are two safe ways to power one from a battery:
 A transfer switch or generator inlet installed by a licensed electrician. Larger home-backup stations are often built to connect this way; check the manufacturer's install guide.
 A furnace power inlet or cord-and-plug connection , where local code allows it, also installed by an electrician. You then plug the furnace straight into the power station during an outage.
 Never plug a power source into a wall outlet to feed power back into the house. This "backfeeding" can energize utility lines and electrocute line workers; OSHA warns it can energize wiring "for great distances." Some furnace control boards also check polarity and grounding before they'll light, so have the electrician test the setup with your actual power station before winter, not during the first outage.
 A battery power station makes no exhaust, so it's safe to keep indoors next to the furnace. A gas generator is not: it belongs outdoors, far from doors and windows, because of carbon monoxide. Our power station vs. gas generator comparison covers the trade-offs for long outages.
 How can you make the battery last longer?
 Turn the thermostat down a few degrees. Fewer cycles means less blower time.
 Close off unused rooms and shut their vents so the house holds heat longer.
 Unplug everything else on the station except essentials like the router and phone chargers.
 Recharge during the day from solar panels or a car if the outage stretches on. Our guide to how many solar panels charge a power station has the math.
 Size the whole outage, not just the furnace. Add the fridge, lights and medical devices with our home backup sizing worksheet .
 FAQ
 Can a 1000W power station run a gas furnace?
 Often, yes, if the furnace runs under about 800W and the station's surge rating covers the blower's startup. Runtime is short, though: a 1,000Wh battery runs a 500W furnace for about 1.7 hours of nonstop blower time.
 Can I plug my furnace into a power station?
 Only if the furnace already has a code-approved cord and plug, or an electrician has installed an inlet or transfer switch. Most furnaces are hardwired, so don't splice cords yourself.
 Does a furnace need a pure sine wave inverter?
 Yes. Furnace control boards, flame sensors and ECM blower motors can fail to light, buzz or lock out on modified sine wave power. Use a pure sine wave power station.
 How many watts does a furnace blower need to start?
 Honda's sizing chart lists about 1,400 starting watts for a 1/3-hp furnace fan and about 2,350 starting watts for a 1/2-hp fan. ECM variable-speed blowers ramp up gently and need much less.
 Will a power station run a furnace all night?
 A 2,000Wh station can usually get a typical furnace through about 7 hours if it cycles half the time, and an efficient ECM furnace much longer. For multi-day outages, plan on 3,000Wh or more, extra batteries, or solar recharging.
 Is it safe to run a power station indoors next to the furnace?
 Yes. A lithium power station produces no fumes, so it can sit indoors. Keep it dry, off the floor if the basement floods, and within its operating temperature range.

 How we got these numbers: runtimes are our calculations from manufacturer-rated capacity with an 85% efficiency factor, not lab tests. The 250W, 500W and 875W loads are example furnace draws based on the ranges above; the "cycling" column assumes the furnace runs about half of each hour. Your furnace's nameplate or a clamp-meter reading is the number to trust. Power station specs come from manufacturer pages (accessed October 2026). See how we research .

Can a Power Station Run a Gas Furnace? Wattage & Hookup Skip to content Prices are approximate and change often, so check the current price before you buy.
 Key takeaways
 A power station can run a gas or propane furnace's blower and controls. It cannot run an electric furnace or electric heat strips, which draw thousands of watts.
 Most furnaces are hardwired. Connecting one means a licensed electrician installing a transfer switch or interlock. Never use extension cords or back-feed a circuit.
 Find the real wattage first. Check the furnace nameplate (amps x volts) or log it with an energy meter. Blowers vary widely, and so does how often they run.
 Runtime is Wh x 0.85 / average watts. A 2,048Wh station at 200W average gives about 8.7 hours. Multi-day outages need a large battery plus solar, or a plan B.
 A furnace is a far better use of a battery than a space heater, but it is still one more load beside the fridge.
